samuell · Oct 17, 2026

I think you are right, and I should have done a search on that before. Found now that FBP inventor cites someone Weinberg from 1975 about them (though FBP is supposed to be from around 69-70, so might be a somewhat parallel discovery):

> Now what are "IN" and "OUT" that our pseudocode receives IPs from and sends them to? They are not the names of connections, as this would tie a component's code to one place in the network, but are things called "ports". "Portae" means "gates" in Latin, and ports (like seaports) can be thought of as specific places in a wall or boundary where things or people go in or out. Weinberg (1975) describes a port as

"... a special place on the boundary through which input and output flow... Only within the location of the port can the dangerous processes of input and output take place, and by so localizing these processes, special mechanisms may be brought to bear on the special problems of input and output."

https://www.jpaulmorrison.com/fbp/concepts_book.shtml

Still, I'm amazed at how it took so long before they became mainstream in data flow oriented libraries and DSLs.

And it seems J.P. Morrison was also highlighting Named ports as particularly useful, which is also perhaps what I should have highlighted in my initial comment above.

It's gotten better lately it seems, but a lot of tools skipped that part, which now requires tons of specialized syntax just for routing of multiple parallel streams.

Jtsummers · Oct 17, 2026

The main thing this seems to provide is determinism. Where Erlang, to stick to your question, can be non-deterministic (without taking special care). I'm reading the dissertation this work is based on to see how it guarantees determinism, so at present I'm just taking their word for it.

https://www2.eecs.berkeley.edu/Pubs/TechRpts/2020/Archive/EE...

In chapter 1 they provide an example of (using Erlang syntax, completely untested so probably needs some massaging to run as I'm rusty on Erlang) this scenario, which would be deterministic in Erlang:

  counter() -> counter(1).
  counter(N) ->
    receive
      dbl -> counter(N*2);
      {inc, Arg} ->
        N1 = N1 + Arg,
        io:format("~w~n", [N1]),
        counter(N1)
    end.

  main() ->
    P = spawn(counter),
    P ! dbl,
    P ! {inc, 1}.
Because messages sent from one process to another are guaranteed to be made available in that same order, this is deterministic. They introduce a motivating example on page 5 (21 in the PDF) where a relay is introduced.

  relay() ->
    receive
      P -> P ! dbl
    end,
    relay(P).

  main_with_relay() ->
    P = spawn(counter),
    R = spawn(relay),
    R ! P,    % <- trouble starts here
    P ! {inc, 1}.
This may give the same result as the first example when run on the same node, but the guarantee is lost, it might not happen in the same order as the first version. For an example where it will likely give a different result, consider if counter were a local process to main (on the same node) while relay were a remote process (on a separate node) with high latency, it's likely that the network delay would result in {inc, 1} arriving before dbl.

The work in LF lets you write this (don't ask me how, still reading) so that the relay would be logically instantaneous even if physically it wasn't, consequently the dbl message would arrive "first" by logical time and the counter would process things as in the original Erlang code.

Of course, you can make the Erlang relay behavior deterministic, but you have to add extra code to achieve it. LF apparently gives you a simpler way to get the desired determinism without having to write the extra code yourself, it's baked into its semantics.

rramadass · Oct 17, 2026

Interesting.

Your use of the word "Reactor" at first confused me since there is a "Reactor Pattern" for event handling (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reactor_pattern) which is not what you mean.

How does your concurrency model differ from that of Erlang (the poster child for distributed concurrency)? Do you have a paper detailing your model and comparing with other languages?

I recently read Roman Obermaisser's excellent book "Event-Triggered and Time-Triggered Control Paradigms" which seems applicable to your architecture. At the bottom most level you have a global communication network based on a synchronized global clock and "Time-Triggered"(TT) semantics which is deterministic. A "Event-Triggered"(ET) communication channel is then overlaid on top of it which is non-deterministic. That way the system provides both hard real-time (i.e. TT) and soft real-time (i.e. ET) semantics.
